curriculumDefinition.commandsAndConcepts: `v`, `V`, `Ctrl-v`; `o`, `O`; `gv`; selection operations `d c y x r ~ u U > < = gq`; Visual Block `I A c d x r` and its ragged right edge `$`; selection increment `Ctrl-a` and `g Ctrl-a`
curriculumDefinition.learningOutcome: Select character, line, and rectangular ranges; modify them, including lines that end in different columns; and decide when selection is clearer than operator-motion
curriculumDefinition.representativeExercises: Indent lines; replace a column marker; prepend text to several rows; reselect and correct the last selection; append past ragged line endings; renumber a reordered list
curriculumDefinition.priorityAndPortability: Core. `Ctrl-v` is semantically important even when a host reserves that chord; the app teaches Vim behavior

lessons.title: Append past ragged ends
lessons.objective: Release the block's right edge with $ so an append or a delete reaches the end of every selected line, whatever length each one is.

activities.title: A block with no right edge
activities.body: A block selection normally has two fixed columns, a left one and a right one. Press `$` while the block is open and the right edge is released: every selected row now runs to its own last character. `A` then appends after each line's end rather than at one shared column, and `d` deletes each line's tail.
activities.contrast: Without `$` the right edge stays where it was, so on lines of different length the text lands inside the code on every row but one.

hints: The block's right edge is a column, and a column cannot follow three different endings.
Watch where the semicolons land rather than how many there are.

feedback.success: Three semicolons landed, and all three landed in the wrong place.
feedback.why: The block's right edge was column one on every row, so the append followed that column instead of each line's last character.
feedback.contrast: The next demo releases that edge and appends to the three real endings.

provenance.languageRationale: JavaScript statements of unequal length make the missed line endings obvious.

activities.title: Terminate a paragraph of statements
activities.instruction: End every statement above the blank line with a semicolon, leaving the call below it untouched.

commandGroups.explanation: Extend the selection to the blank line that ends the paragraph.
Pull the selection back off the blank line.
Release the right edge so every row runs to its own end.
Append text after each line's last character.
Replicate the terminator onto the three statement endings.

checkpoints.caption: The paragraph motion lands on the blank line.

hints: A paragraph motion reaches the blank line itself, which is one row too far.
A blank line has an end too, and it would take a semicolon.

feedback.success: Three statements terminated, and the blank line left alone.
feedback.why: The paragraph motion sized the block, one row back excluded the blank line, and the released right edge reached three different endings.

provenance.languageRationale: A JavaScript paragraph followed by a blank line is where this block idiom is normally used.

activities.title: Reach the ends
activities.prompt: A block spans four lines of different length and every line needs a semicolon at its own end. Which key belongs in the sequence?

options.label: Nothing; `A` already appends at each end

activities.explanation: `A` appends at the block's right edge, which is a fixed column until `$` releases it.

lessons.title: Number a selected column
lessons.objective: Increment every number in a selection, uniformly with Ctrl-a or as a running sequence with g Ctrl-a.

activities.title: One chord, every number
activities.body: `Ctrl-a` adds one to the number under the cursor. Over a Visual selection it adds one to the first number on every selected line at once. Prefix it with `g` and the amount added grows line by line: the first selected line gains one, the second gains two, and a column of identical numbers becomes a sequence.
activities.grammar: v/V/Ctrl-v + rows + Ctrl-a or g Ctrl-a
activities.contrast: `Ctrl-a` moves a whole column by the same amount; `g Ctrl-a` spreads it into 1, 2, 3. Renumbering a list after a reorder is the second one.

activities.title: Move a whole column by one
activities.instruction: Watch three identical ports move up together.

commandGroups.explanation: Move two lines down to extend the selection.
Add one to the first number on every selected line.

checkpoints.caption: Every line gained the same one.

hints: The selection decides which numbers are in scope.
Each line gains the same amount.

feedback.success: All three ports moved by one.
feedback.why: Over a selection the increment applies once to each selected line, with the same amount every time.

provenance.languageRationale: Repeated port settings are a familiar column of identical numbers.

activities.title: Spread the same column into a sequence
activities.instruction: Watch the same three ports become three different ports.

commandGroups.explanation: Move two lines down to extend the selection.
Add a growing amount, so the selected lines become a sequence.

checkpoints.caption: The first line gained one, the second two, the third three.

hints: Only one key separates this from the previous demo.
Compare how much each line gained, not whether it changed.

feedback.success: One column became three distinct ports.
feedback.why: The `g` prefix makes the amount cumulative down the selection, which is what turns identical numbers into a sequence.

provenance.languageRationale: Reusing the previous demo's buffer isolates the `g` prefix as the only difference.

activities.title: Renumber a reordered list
activities.instruction: The steps were reordered and every marker now reads one. Number them one through five again, working from the second step down.

commandGroups.explanation: Switch to Visual Line mode on the second step.
Move three lines down to cover the remaining steps.
Add a growing amount, so the selected markers become 2, 3, 4, 5.

hints: The first step already carries the number it should keep.
The second step needs to gain one, the third two.

feedback.success: Five steps, five numbers, one command.
feedback.why: Leaving the first marker out of the selection makes the growing amount line up with the numbers the list needs.

provenance.languageRationale: A Markdown ordered list is where duplicated markers survive a reorder.

activities.title: Raise three defaults together
activities.instruction: Raise all three shell defaults from five to fifteen, keeping them equal.

commandGroups.explanation: Move two lines down to extend the selection.
Count how much every selected number should gain.
Add that amount to the first number on every selected line.

hints: The three defaults must stay equal, so the amount added must not grow.
A count in front of the increment sets how much is added.

feedback.success: Three defaults raised by ten, still equal.
feedback.why: A count sets the amount, and without the growing prefix every selected line gains that same amount.

provenance.languageRationale: Shell defaults are tuned together, which is the case for the uniform form.

activities.title: Number an aligned enum
activities.instruction: Give the four aligned Python constants the distinct values one through four.

commandGroups.explanation: Switch to Visual Block mode on the value column.
Move three lines down to cover the whole column.
Add a growing amount, so the column becomes 1, 2, 3, 4.

checkpoints.caption: The block covers the value column and nothing else.

hints: The constants are padded so their values share a column.
The same growing increment works whatever shape selected the numbers.

feedback.why: A rectangular selection picked out the value column, and the growing increment numbered it in one command.

provenance.languageRationale: Aligned Python constants pair the column selection with the increment in one workflow.

activities.title: Give four rows distinct keys
activities.instruction: Every inserted row carries the placeholder key zero. Turn the whole column into the distinct keys one through four.

commandGroups.explanation: Extend the selection to the last row.
Add a growing amount, so the placeholders become 1, 2, 3, 4.

hints: Every row starts at zero, so the first row must gain one as well.
A uniform increase would leave all four keys equal, which is what a key cannot be.

feedback.success: Four placeholder keys became four distinct keys.
feedback.why: Because every row started from the same placeholder, the growing increment produced exactly the sequence the column needed.

provenance.languageRationale: Placeholder keys in a SQL insert are a routine renumbering target.

activities.title: Same amount or growing amount
activities.prompt: Four selected lines each read `0`. Which command leaves them reading 1, 2, 3, 4?
activities.explanation: `Ctrl-a` adds the same amount to every selected line, and a count only changes what that shared amount is. The `g` prefix is what makes the amount grow line by line.

lessons.title: Choose when selection is clearer
lessons.objective: Combine selection shapes and operations, then choose Visual mode only when seeing the range improves confidence.

activities.title: Use Visual mode when seeing the range helps
activities.body: Use an operator and motion when the target is easy to name. Use Visual mode when you need to check an irregular range or edit a rectangle before committing.
activities.grammar: known range → operator-motion · inspect first → Visual · columns → Ctrl-v
activities.contrast: The best choice exposes intent without unnecessary setup.

activities.title: Match each shape to its target
activities.instruction: Uppercase one call name, then indent the two statements that belong to the branch.

commandGroups.explanation: Extend the selection to the end of the call name.
Move one line down to extend the selection.

hints: A word inside a row and a pair of whole rows are different shapes.
Choose the shape that matches each target before operating.

feedback.success: Two targets, two shapes, one buffer.
feedback.why: The name needed a character selection and the rows needed a linewise one.

provenance.languageRationale: A small Python block puts a word target and a line-range target side by side.

activities.title: Repair and normalize assignments
activities.instruction: Turn all three annotations into assignments, then uppercase the first variable name.

commandGroups.explanation: Move two lines down to extend the selection.
Replace every character in the block selection.
Move to the start of the first assignment.
Extend the selection to the end of the variable name.

hints: Choose the selection shape before moving.
Apply the operation only after the intended range is highlighted.

feedback.why: The selection made the affected text explicit before the operation.

provenance.languageRationale: Aligned Python annotations support a block repair followed by a characterwise normalization.

activities.title: Reselect and normalize labels
activities.instruction: Toggle all three labels, then reselect the same rows and normalize them to uppercase.

commandGroups.explanation: Move two lines down to extend the selection.
Toggle the case of the selected lines.

hints: Choose the selection shape before moving.
Apply the operation only after the intended range is highlighted.

feedback.why: The selection made the affected text explicit before the operation.

provenance.languageRationale: YAML-style labels keep the restored line range visually obvious while case changes compose.

activities.title: Fix one call and drop its stale copy
activities.instruction: Replace the leading argument of the first Go call with “active”, then remove the stale call on the row below.

commandGroups.explanation: Extend the selection to just before the comma.
Change the selected argument in Insert mode.
Move down to the stale call.

hints: The argument is a fragment of a row; the stale call is an entire row.
Each of the two targets wants a different selection shape.

feedback.success: One argument replaced, one whole row gone.
feedback.why: A character selection bounded the argument, and a linewise selection took the row entire.

provenance.languageRationale: A repeated Go call offers a punctuation-bounded argument beside a redundant whole row.

activities.title: Normalize one inspected argument
activities.instruction: Uppercase the first Ruby call argument while leaving its comma and the second argument unchanged.

commandGroups.explanation: Extend the selection to just before the comma.

hints: Inspect the visible punctuation-bounded range before changing it.
Keep the comma outside the selection.

feedback.success: Only the inspected Ruby argument changed case.
feedback.why: Visual Character made the exact range visible before the transformation.

provenance.languageRationale: A Ruby call provides a compact range whose visible punctuation supports deliberate selection.

activities.title: Choose the clearer method
activities.prompt: You know the exact text object for one quoted value and do not need to inspect it first. Which approach is usually clearer?

options.label: Use an operator with the text object

activities.explanation: When the range is already precise and nameable, operator-motion or operator-object grammar is usually simpler.

activities.title: Select with a reason
activities.body: Choose a shape that matches the text, inspect the range, then apply one deliberate operation. Reuse `o`, `O`, and `gv` when the range—not the editing idea—needs adjustment.
takeaways: `v`, `V`, and `Ctrl-v` select characters, lines, and rectangles.
`o` and `O` move the active endpoint; `gv` restores the last selection.
Visual Block `I` and `A` apply one insertion across several rows.
Prefer operator-motion when the range is already clear; use Visual mode when seeing it reduces risk.

reference.purpose: Enter characterwise, linewise, or blockwise Visual mode.
notes: The mode determines the geometry of the highlighted range.

reference.purpose: Move the active end or block corner.
notes: `O` is specifically useful in Visual Block.
The previous shape and extent are restored.

reference.purpose: Delete, change, capture, remove, or fill the selected range.
notes: The register shape follows the Visual selection shape.

reference.purpose: Toggle, lowercase, or uppercase the selection.
notes: In Visual mode, `u` lowercases rather than undoing.

reference.purpose: Shift, reindent, or format selected lines.
notes: Visual Line is the natural shape for these activities.

reference.purpose: Insert at the left or right edge of every block row.
notes: Press Escape to replicate the typed insertion.

reference.purpose: Release the block right edge so every row runs to its own end.
notes: The left edge stays fixed, so the rows still need a shared starting column.
It applies to the append and to the delete alike.

reference.purpose: Increment the first number on every selected line.
notes: A count sets the amount; without `g` every selected line gains that same amount.
`g` makes the amount cumulative, which turns identical numbers into a sequence.
`Ctrl-x` and `g Ctrl-x` subtract in the same two ways.
